visuals.heading: Failure and Shutdown Numbers

items.text: "Startups are risky" gets said so often it stops meaning anything.
Here is how that played out over the last few years.

A study by the Institute of Business Value and Oxford Economics found roughly 90% of Indian startups fail within their first five years, a success rate near 10%, well below the global average of about 33%.
Misreading market demand accounts for roughly 42% of startup failures in India, followed by a weak founding team (about 23%) and being outpaced by competitors (about 19%).
Indian startup funding fell sharply from its 2021 peak as global capital tightened.
Total startup funding in India fell to a seven-year low, down roughly 60-62% from 2022 depending on the tracker.

blocks.heading: Equity Is the Part of a Startup

items.text: The standard Indian structure is a 1-year cliff followed by vesting over roughly 4 years, about 25% a year.

Vested options only become shares once you exercise them, and exercising means paying the strike price plus a perquisite tax on the gain, in cash, at the moment you exercise, before you have sold anything or seen a rupee of that value.
If your startup employer runs out of funding or has a bad quarter, how many months could your household absorb a sudden job search without real financial stress.
This is not about whether the startup looks stable today.

blocks.heading: How the Risk Changes By Startup Stage

items.text: "Startup job" covers everything from a six-person seed-stage team to a pre-IPO company with thousands of employees.
Cash pay is usually the lowest relative to market rate, and the company itself may not survive its next fundraise, early-stage failure is where most of the 90% five-year failure rate concentrates.

blocks.heading: Mistakes to Avoid When Making This Decision

items.text: An early-stage startup with six months of runway and a late-stage, well-funded startup with a clear path to IPO carry completely different risk profiles, even though both get called "a startup job" in the same sentence.

Accepting a lower cash CTC because the ESOP number on the offer letter "makes up the difference" only works if the company survives to a liquidity event, you survive to your vesting cliff, and you have the cash to exercise when the time comes.
People research a startup's last funding round in detail and never run the same math on their own household, how many months of expenses they could cover if that role disappeared tomorrow.
